title: Turn 10,994 Notes Into Memory - Paul Iusztin, Decoding AI & Louis-François Bouchard, Towards AI

primary.label: Context Engineering & Memory
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 65%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's core object is a file-based memory layer that organizes what enters model context and persists state across agent sessions, fitting context engineering and memory. The AI Research OS is a personal system used daily across articles, videos, codebases, and courses without a single vertical focus. The system has been iterated over 18 months through three major versions and is used daily in production by the authors. The content targets engineers comfortable with agent harnesses, CLIs, and multi-agent design but not cutting-edge research. The session is a hands-on workshop with three live demos and a course tie-in.

summary: Paul and Louis-François built the AI Research OS over 18 months through three major iterations. Version 1 was scoped for their agent engineering course: given a topic and manually handpicked golden links, a deep research algorithm with an orchestrator agent generated queries, dispatched sub-agents using Gemini grounded in Google Search, ran three rounds of six queries each (40-50 links), ranked sources against the topic, fully scraped the top K, and compiled everything into a static research.md file. This generated 35 lessons quickly but was limited. Version 2 targeted the Second Brain itself — Obsidian, Readwise, NotebookLM, GitHub — instead of only the public web, eliminating the need for manually curated golden links. But the output was still a static file requiring expensive re-runs for any new question. Version 3 added a wiki layer on top of the deep research pipeline: sources in, wiki out. Raw files are stored individually, an index.yaml catalog provides summaries and metadata, and an LLM-generated wiki of derivatives (comparisons, concepts, entities, notes, open questions) sits on top. They rejected vector databases, knowledge graphs, and semantic search in favor of plain files and references for simplicity. The wiki is token-efficient: the agent reads index.yaml first, then source wiki pages (executive summaries), then wiki derivatives, and only reads full raw sources as a last resort. The wiki is alive — every question leaves a trace, creating new concept, note, or comparison files. Three demos showcase the system: (1) deep research on agentic AI engineering from a brain dump plus references, producing a wiki with comparisons, concepts, entities, and source executive summaries; (2) ingesting three GitHub repositories (OpenCode, Py, Hermes) by auto-cloning and generating per-repo notes plus higher-level architectural comparisons; (3) ingesting custom web links with minimal setup requiring only Git and curl. Projects can be articles, videos, slides, books, courses, or tracking a whole codebase. The system remains a builder workflow (terminal-based, no polished UI) by design, with the goal of teaching AI engineering. Future improvements include more connectors (Google Drive, Notion, Slack), better source provenance, memory compaction, and stronger linting. Their Agent Engineering course (~60 hours) teaches similar deep research and multi-agent system building.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.
temporalContext: Transcript claims reflect the publication date; linked external context was checked at the run's research date.
takeaways: The system evolved through three versions: V1 produced static research.md files from golden links; V2 targeted the Second Brain directly; V3 added a living wiki layer on top of raw files and an index.

The deep research algorithm uses an orchestrator agent that generates queries, dispatches sub-agents to search Google (via Gemini), runs multiple rounds, ranks sources by signal, fully scrapes the top K, and summarizes the rest.

Version 3 replaces static output with a queryable wiki: raw files stored individually, an index.yaml catalog with metadata and summaries, and LLM-generated wiki derivatives (comparisons, concepts, entities, notes, open questions).
They deliberately rejected vector databases, knowledge graphs, and semantic search in favor of plain files and references for a simpler, lighter personal system.
Token-efficient querying follows a hierarchy: read index.yaml first, then source wiki pages (executive summaries), then wiki derivatives, and only read full raw sources as a last resort.

The wiki is alive and evolves with every question — each question can create new concept, note, or comparison files, and all questions are logged, creating a reflection of the user's thinking over time.
Deep research depth options (light/deep/fast) control query rounds and count: light does 1 round of 3 queries, fast does 2 rounds of 3 queries; the process takes 10-20 minutes.
The system is a builder workflow by design — terminal-based with no polished UI/UX — because the goal is to teach AI engineering, not build a commercial product.
GitHub repository ingestion auto-clones repos and generates per-repo architectural notes plus higher-level cross-repo comparisons, useful for learning or writing new harnesses.
Custom link ingestion works with minimal setup (just Git and curl), requiring no Obsidian, Readwise, or other service dependencies.

sections.title: Introduction: The Second Brain Problem
sections.summary: Paul introduces his Second Brain of 5,000+ Obsidian notes and 5,000+ Readwise notes growing at 250 files/month. His core problem: losing research, a graveyard reading list, and the desire for a system anchored to personal notes and values. He introduces the AI Research OS.

sections.title: Speaker Introductions
sections.summary: Paul introduces himself as founder/CEO of Decoding AI and co-author of the LLM Engineer's Handbook. Louis-François introduces himself as co-founder/CTO of Towards AI, creator of What's AI YouTube, and former PhD student.

sections.title: Choosing the Right Tool for Research
sections.summary: Louis-François outlines a tool-selection hierarchy: Google/ChatGPT for quick queries; Codex/Claude Code for small one-off tasks; NotebookLM for content digestion (not ownable, not agent-native, weak for coding); RAG/vector DBs for production (infrastructure-heavy, not human-friendly). For personalized, compounding, inspectable research, building a custom system is the answer.

sections.title: The Context Window Bottleneck and File-Based Solution
sections.summary: The core insight: the bottleneck is not providing more context but leveraging it in the future. With agents, the context window is everything and it's lost when the conversation stops. They chose plain markdown files as a memory layer that is both human- and agent-friendly.

sections.title: Moving Data to Obsidian and the AI Research OS Repository
sections.summary: Louis-François consolidated all scattered data into Obsidian for local, cross-platform access. The AI Research OS repo provides Claude Code and Codex skills/plugins for deep research, search, and distillation across Obsidian, Readwise, NotebookLM, GitHub, YouTube, web links, and documents.

sections.title: Version 1: Deep Research for Course Lessons
sections.summary: Paul explains V1: input was a topic plus manually handpicked golden links; a deep research algorithm used an orchestrator agent to generate queries, dispatched sub-agents using Gemini grounded in Google Search, ran 3 rounds of 6 queries each (40-50 links), ranked sources against the topic, fully scraped top K, and compiled everything into a static research.md file. This generated 35 lessons quickly but was limited to the public web.

sections.title: Version 2: Targeting the Second Brain
sections.summary: V2 aimed the deep research loop at the Second Brain (Obsidian, Readwise, NotebookLM, GitHub) instead of only the public web, eliminating the need for manually curated golden links. But the output was still a static research.md file requiring expensive full re-runs for any new question.

sections.title: Version 3: Adding the Wiki Layer
sections.summary: V3 added a wiki layer (LLM knowledge base) on top of the deep research pipeline: sources in, wiki out. Raw files are stored individually, an index.yaml catalog is created, and a queryable wiki of derivatives is generated. They rejected vector databases, knowledge graphs, and semantic search in favor of plain files and references for simplicity.

sections.title: The File-Based Index and Wiki Structure
sections.summary: The index.yaml file is a catalog of all data with summaries and metadata (origin, title, authors, publication date). The wiki has a raw folder (immutable source data), a wiki folder (LLM-generated derivatives: comparisons, concepts, entities, notes, open questions), and the index pointing to everything. As the wiki grows, connections between entities and concepts emerge visually in Obsidian.

sections.title: Token-Efficient Querying and the Living Wiki
sections.summary: Querying follows a hierarchy: agent reads index.yaml first, then source wiki pages (executive summaries), then wiki derivatives, and only reads full raw sources as a last resort — making it token-efficient. The wiki is alive: every question leaves a trace, creating new concept/note/comparison files and logging all questions. Paul uses the PARA method so Obsidian remains an immutable snapshot the LLM never touches; the wiki is scoped per project through deep research or targeted ingestion.

sections.title: Projects and Skills Setup
sections.summary: Projects can be anything — articles, videos, slides, books, courses, or tracking a whole codebase. The project is the work; the Second Brain is the research. Skills are packed as a Cloud Code plugin but can be adapted to any harness. Setup requires additional dependencies (Obsidian, Readwise, NotebookLM CLIs and authentication) detailed in the README.

sections.title: Demo 1: Researching Agentic AI Engineering
sections.summary: Starting from a brain dump file plus selected references, the research skill is triggered via Claude Code. Depth options (light/deep/fast) control query rounds and count; light does 1 round of 3 queries, fast does 2 rounds of 3. The process takes 10-20 minutes, scanning Obsidian, Readwise, and NotebookLM. The output wiki contains raw files, index (visible as Obsidian graph), and wiki derivatives: comparisons (e.g., agentic RAG vs. file systems), concepts (e.g., agent loop with summaries containing graphs and tags), entities, and source executive summaries computed once during ingestion.

sections.title: Demo 2: Ingesting and Comparing GitHub Repositories
sections.summary: Three open-source repos (OpenCode, Py, Hermes) are ingested to learn harness engineering. No deep research — just ingestion on specified topics (architecture, sub-agents, memory system, permission flow). The system auto-clones repos, generates per-repo notes explaining architecture, then creates higher-level cross-repo comparisons and aggregated concept files. Useful for understanding architectural differences or writing a new harness.

sections.title: Demo 3: Ingesting Custom Web Links
sections.summary: The simplest example: ingesting three custom random links. Works with no Obsidian, Readwise, or other service setup — only Git and curl. Produces index, source executive summaries, extracted concepts, and entities. Demonstrates the system's minimal-infrastructure entry point.

sections.title: Querying and Growing the Wiki
sections.summary: Asking questions on top of an existing wiki (e.g., about sandboxing in harness engineering) triggers the agent to query the wiki, provide an answer, and update the wiki with new notes, comparisons, or entities — keeping the wiki alive and evolving.

sections.title: Future Improvements and Agent Engineering Course
sections.summary: Future improvements include more connectors (Google Drive, Notion, Slack), better source provenance for ranking and reuse, memory compaction, and stronger linting. The system remains a builder workflow (terminal-based, no polished UI) by design — the goal is teaching AI engineering, not building a product. Their Agent Engineering course (~60 hours) teaches similar deep research and multi-agent system building with a final project.

demonstrations: Demo 1 — Researching agentic AI engineering: Starting from a brain dump file plus selected references, the deep research skill is triggered via Claude Code. Choosing 'light' depth (1 round, 3 queries), the process takes 10-20 minutes, scanning Obsidian, Readwise, and NotebookLM. Output wiki contains raw files, index, and wiki derivatives: comparisons (e.g., agentic RAG vs. file systems, compaction vs. recursive language models), concepts (e.g., agent loop), entities, and source executive summaries.

Demo 2 — Ingesting GitHub repositories: Three open-source repos (OpenCode, Py, Hermes) are ingested on harness engineering topics (general architecture, sub-agents, memory system, permission flow). The system auto-clones repos, generates per-repo notes on architecture, then creates higher-level cross-repo comparisons and aggregated concept files. Useful for understanding architectural differences or writing a new harness.

Demo 3 — Ingesting custom web links: The simplest setup — ingesting three random custom links with no Obsidian, Readwise, or other service dependencies, only requiring Git and curl. Produces index, source executive summaries, extracted concepts, and entities. Demonstrates the system works with minimal infrastructure.
